title: World Wide Web proposal: start with the organization’s information problem
focus: A concept becomes credible when it explains the users, existing assets, adoption constraints, and deliberate scope boundaries.

sources.title: Tim Berners-Lee, Information Management: A Proposal
sources.locator: Losing Information at CERN; CERN Requirements; Non requirements; A Practical Project
sources.limitations: Author-hosted HTML transcription of the original proposal. It is evidence of intent, not proof that every proposed feature was implemented or widely adopted.

facts.statement: The proposal addresses information loss and relationships across a changing organization, then calls for heterogeneous access, decentralization, and links to existing data.
facts.locator: Losing Information at CERN; CERN Requirements

facts.statement: It treats sophisticated authorization and accounting as outside the proposed local scope while discussing use of existing protection for protected data.

retrospective.boundary: Researchers, institutional memory, existing databases, diverse computers, links, and local adoption form the proposed information system.
interfaces: Existing repository → new access layer: adoption depends on useful information being available early.
Local collaboration → broader deployment: a changed trust environment can invalidate deliberate scope exclusions.

decision.question: How should a team assess a promising early concept?
options: Score it by the eventual market’s feature list.
Evaluate problem fit, adoption path, alternatives, and the assumptions that must hold in its initial context.
decision.recommendation: Keep the initial scope coherent while recording conditions that trigger redesign.
decision.uncertainty: The later success of the Web does not prove each early design choice was inevitable or universally appropriate.

rows: Preserve relationships across people, projects, and repositories
Expose useful existing material before requiring migration
Reopen protection and governance when access expands
New users, threats, obligations, and ownership

questions: Why is access to existing information an architectural requirement rather than only a convenience?
When is a non-requirement responsible scoping, and when does it become a dangerous inherited assumption?
Pitch a small pilot without using eventual success as evidence available in 1989.
answer_signals: Frames the problem in organizational work rather than a technology label.
Recognizes adoption and compatibility as system constraints.
Keeps historical context distinct from present-day security needs.
retrospective.transfer_exercise: Synthetic: propose a shared engineering knowledge service for three teams using incompatible repositories. Include one deliberate exclusion and its reopening trigger.
retrospective.limits: This is analysis of the original proposal, not a claim about all subsequent Web standards or a current security recommendation.
